strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: reconciling physical constraint satisfaction with distributional accuracy in generative surrogate modeling, which is important for UQ in engineering/physics applications.

Extensive empirical validation across three benchmarks of increasing complexity (steady-state Darcy flow, transient Kolmogorov flow, and a highly complex multi-field compressible dynamic stall problem), covering all three residual categories described (steady-state, conservation-type, and algebraic).

Careful and honest comparison against strong baselines (PIDM-ME, CoCoGen, DM), including a valuable diagnostic showing that PIDM-ME's apparently low residual error is an artifact of a degenerate, narrow-range pressure distribution rather than true fidelity — this is a useful and non-trivial finding.

Good set of ablations: effect of unrolling steps, σmin, timestep sampling distribution (uniform vs logit-normal), stochastic vs deterministic samplers, residual weighting power law, and DiT vs UNet backbone — providing practical guidance for practitioners.

Reports both accuracy gains and computational costs (training overhead vs. unchanged inference cost), and includes a meaningful comparison of surrogate inference time vs. full CPU-based numerical simulation on the dynamic stall case, underscoring practical value.
Framework generalizes to different residual types and conditioning setups, suggesting reasonably broad applicability.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is somewhat limited: the conflict-free gradient update (ConFIG) is adopted essentially unchanged from prior work (Liu et al., 2025a), and the logit-normal timestep sampling is borrowed from Esser et al. (2024); the main new components are the application of these ideas to flow matching plus unrolling, which is a comparatively modest contribution given the paper's framing as a 'unified framework.'

The magnitude of improvement varies substantially across benchmarks (e.g., only ~1.05–1.68× reduction for Kolmogorov flow vs. up to 8× for dynamic stall), and the paper does not deeply analyze why the benefit is so much smaller in the turbulent/conservation-law setting, which is arguably the most scientifically interesting case.

The logit-normal time-sampling ablation shows no clear benefit over uniform sampling (Darcy flow results), yet it's still promoted as a contribution/technique without strong justification for inclusion beyond precedent from image generation.

Training-time computational overhead is non-trivial (up to ~4-5× cost with 4 unrolling steps and ConFIG combined) but the paper does not analyze accuracy vs. compute trade-offs in a Pareto sense, nor discuss how these costs scale with model/problem size.

The toy circle experiment and some visual/qualitative results (e.g., mean/std comparisons) rely on relatively small sample counts (128 or fewer) for turbulent/complex problems, raising questions about statistical robustness of reported gains, especially for distributional metrics like Wasserstein distance.

Limited theoretical grounding for why conflict-free gradient combination is specifically well-suited to the flow-matching (vs. diffusion) setting beyond empirical demonstration; the paper would benefit from more rigorous analysis of convergence properties or guarantees under the proposed scheme.

Comparisons to CoCoGen and PIDM-ME, while informative, are somewhat narrow (only Darcy flow) and it is unclear if similar failure modes/success patterns would be observed on the other two benchmarks, limiting generality of the comparative claims.

The claims of "first integration of flow matching in a framework that embeds physical principles with high accuracy" are strong and could be tempered, as similar residual-embedding ideas already exist for diffusion models (PIDM, CoCoGen) and the delta here is primarily the conflict-free combination + unrolling.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across three diverse PDE problems (steady-state Darcy flow, transient Kolmogorov flow, and complex multi-field dynamic stall), covering the three stated categories of physical residuals.

Good set of baselines (DM, PIDM-ME, CoCoGen) and careful qualitative critique of the PIDM-ME baseline's apparent residual 'gaming' via distributional collapse, which is a useful observation for the community.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (unrolling steps, power-law weighting of residual loss, sigma_min, logit-normal vs uniform time sampling, deterministic vs stochastic samplers, ConFIG vs fixed loss weighting) that help build intuition for design choices.

Practical relevance is demonstrated via a realistic and computationally expensive dynamic stall CFD application, with inference speed-up analysis showing negligible added cost at sampling time despite training overhead.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed appendices describing dataset generation, architecture/hyperparameters, and residual computation procedures.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing techniques (ConFIG for conflict-free gradients from Liu et al. 2025a, algorithm unrolling from Monga et al. 2021, logit-normal time sampling from Esser et al. 2024) applied to the flow matching + physics-residual setting; the incremental nature of the method over Bastek et al. (2025) and ConFIG is not strongly differentiated beyond application context.

Quantitative results are presented almost exclusively via figures/violin plots without corresponding precise numerical tables for the main comparisons, making exact reported improvements (e.g., the '8x' residual reduction) difficult to verify or reproduce precisely.

No indication of variance across multiple training seeds/runs; single-run comparisons for stochastic training procedures (especially with sensitive multi-objective gradient balancing) raise concerns about the robustness/significance of the reported gains.

The claim of avoiding hyperparameter tuning is somewhat overstated -- there remain several manually chosen hyperparameters (unrolling curriculum schedule, power exponent p, the stochastic sampler threshold t*, sigma_min), even if some are argued to generalize across cases.
The toy circle-constraint ablation (Fig. 2) is very simplistic and provides limited insight into how the method scales to genuinely high-dimensional, more complex constraint interactions.

The 1D pixel-wise Wasserstein distance used to assess distributional accuracy is a weak proxy for full spatial/joint distributional fidelity, a limitation acknowledged by the authors but not otherwise mitigated with stronger distributional metrics.

The 'uncertainty' in the dynamic stall dataset is introduced via a simplistic 2% Gaussian perturbation of nominal simulation parameters rather than reflecting genuine physical/aleatoric variability, which weakens claims about uncertainty quantification relevance.

Limited theoretical justification for why gradient-conflict-free updates (ConFIG) should yield both accurate residuals and high distributional fidelity simultaneously beyond the empirical demonstration; the argument remains largely heuristic.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: reconciling physical constraint satisfaction with distributional accuracy in generative surrogate modeling for PDEs.

Principled use of conflict-free gradient updates (ConFIG) to combine flow-matching and residual losses without manual weight tuning, with an ablation (Appendix E/Fig. 20) showing this consistently outperforms fixed-weight baselines.

Introduces temporal unrolling to obtain more accurate noise-free predictions for residual evaluation at training time, with clear evidence (Darcy, Kolmogorov, dynamic stall) that it substantially reduces residual error without affecting inference cost.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three diverse and representative PDE problems (steady-state, transient/conditioned, and multi-field algebraic-constrained), each with different residual types, which strengthens generality claims.

Careful and honest comparison with strong baselines (PIDM-ME, CoCoGen, DM), including the insightful diagnosis that PIDM-ME's apparently low residual comes from a degenerate/narrow output distribution rather than true fidelity.

Thorough ablations on sigma_min, time-sampling distribution (uniform vs logit-normal), stochastic vs deterministic sampling, and residual weighting power law (Appendix D), giving practical guidance to future work.

Good engineering detail and reproducibility support: detailed dataset generation procedures, architecture/hyperparameter tables, and wall-clock performance comparisons (training vs inference cost, and comparison with the CFD solver).
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines existing components (flow matching, ConFIG conflict-free multi-task optimization from Liu et al. 2025a, and algorithm unrolling) rather than introducing fundamentally new theory or algorithms.

The magnitude of improvement varies substantially across test cases (1.05x-1.68x for Kolmogorov flow vs 8x for dynamic stall), and the paper does not deeply analyze why the method is much less effective when the residual only partially captures the governing physics (as in Kolmogorov flow, where only mass conservation is enforced).

Distributional accuracy is assessed mainly via 1D Wasserstein distance computed per-pixel, which the authors acknowledge ignores full 2D spatial/joint structure; no more holistic distributional metric (e.g., FID-like or spectral) is used to corroborate claims of 'clearly outperforming' baselines in distributional accuracy.

No comparison against other well-known multi-task/conflict-resolution gradient methods (e.g., PCGrad, GradNorm, MGDA) beyond fixed-weight summation, making it unclear whether ConFIG's benefits are specific or would be matched by simpler alternative conflict-resolution schemes.

Unrolling increases training cost non-trivially (up to ~2x for 4 unrolling steps, Table 3), and while inference cost is unaffected, the practical training overhead versus the accuracy gains is not deeply discussed for larger-scale/production settings.

Ablation studies (e.g., power-law scaling, sampler analysis) are conducted only on one or two of the three benchmark problems (e.g., dynamic stall for scaling laws), limiting confidence that conclusions generalize across problem types.

Some figures/results lack quantitative statistical rigor (e.g., limited repetition/seed variation is unclear for many single-run comparisons), and error bars in violin plots refer only to variability within the validation set, not training stochasticity.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three diverse and representative PDE benchmarks (steady-state Darcy flow, transient Kolmogorov flow, and complex multi-field dynamic stall), with consistent metrics (residual error, Wasserstein distance, JS divergence, NFE, inference time).

Extensive ablation studies in the appendix (residual loss scaling laws, sigma_min sensitivity, stochastic sampler threshold, conflict-free vs fixed-weight loss balancing, unrolling depth, loss decomposition variants) that substantiate design choices rather than just presenting a final method.

Clear identification and empirical demonstration of the physics-vs-distribution Pareto trade-off, with a well-organized comparison table (Table 1) situating the method against many recent baselines (FFM, CoCoGen, DiffusionPDE, D-Flow, ECI, PIDM, PIDDM, PCFM, etc.).

Practical significance is well argued: the dynamic stall case is tied to a real industrial simulation (ANSYS Fluent RANS solver) with a meaningful ~week-to-seconds acceleration argument for surrogate modeling and uncertainty quantification.

The method avoids increasing inference cost (a key practical advantage over inference-time correction approaches like CoCoGen, PCFM, D-Flow) while achieving competitive or superior physical/distributional accuracy at training-time cost only.
Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations (training memory/time overhead from unrolling) and negative/neutral ablation results (e.g., splitting physics losses does not help).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing techniques (ConFIG for conflict-free gradients, unrolling, logit-normal time sampling from SD3, stochastic resampling akin to ECI) adapted to physics-constrained flow matching, rather than a fundamentally new method; novelty is more integrative/engineering than conceptual.

The claim of being "the first to recognize the trade-off" between distributional and physical accuracy is overstated, since cited related works (e.g., Krishnapriyan et al. 2021, PIDM, PIDDM) already discuss this conflict, and the paper's own related-work section acknowledges several works grappling with this exact issue.

Baseline coverage is inconsistent across benchmarks: PIDM-ME and CoCoGen are compared only on Darcy flow, and PCFM only on dynamic stall, making it hard to assess relative performance of PBFM against the full baseline set uniformly across all three tasks.

No theoretical guarantee is provided that the ConFIG-based updates or unrolling actually yield Pareto-optimal solutions in a rigorous sense; "Pareto-optimal" is used loosely based on empirical dominance over a small set of compared points rather than a formal optimality characterization.

Training overhead from unrolling is nontrivial (up to ~2.5x time and ~3x memory in Table 6), which may limit scalability to larger 3D or higher-resolution physical systems not tested here; this scalability concern is acknowledged but not empirically explored beyond the three benchmark resolutions used.

The choice of hyperparameters (e.g., t* = 0.2 for the stochastic sampler, p=1 scaling) appears tuned per-benchmark via grid search over validation metrics without a principled selection criterion, raising some concern about how well these choices would transfer to new problems without similar extensive tuning.

Some presented numbers appear to be selectively favorable to the proposed method (e.g., the D-Flow instability filtering of invalid samples in Darcy, various best-selected checkpoints), which could bias the comparison somewhat, though this is disclosed in footnotes.

strengths: The paper provides an extensive empirical evaluation across three distinct PDE benchmarks (steady-state Darcy flow, transient Kolmogorov flow, and complex multi-field dynamic stall), each requiring different residual formulations (finite differences, FFT-based, point-wise).

A large number of ablations are performed: unrolling step count, sigma_min noise-level sensitivity, residual time-weighting power law, stochastic sampler threshold t*, architecture comparison (DiT vs UNet), and loss decomposition (single vs 3-loss variants), which gives useful practical guidance for practitioners.

The method is training-time only, so inference cost is not increased relative to vanilla flow matching, which is a meaningful practical advantage over inference-time correction baselines like PCFM/CoCoGen/D-Flow that are shown to be 10-65x slower at inference.

The paper situates itself clearly against a large body of related work with a useful comparison table (Table 1), and includes a toy problem (circle-constraint) that provides intuition for why each component (ConFIG, unrolling, stochastic sampling) helps.
Reasonably thorough analysis of gradient conflict (cosine similarity measurements) supporting the choice of using ConFIG over fixed-weight loss combinations.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim is overstated: the paper asserts it is 'the first to recognize the trade-off between distributional and physical accuracy,' yet the related work section itself cites PIDM (Bastek et al. 2025), PIDDM (Zhang & Zou 2025), and Krishnapriyan et al. (2021) as already identifying and addressing this very conflict with weighted losses, undermining the claimed primary contribution.

The core technical contribution is essentially an assembly of three pre-existing techniques (ConFIG from Liu et al. 2025a, unrolling, and a stochastic sampler similar to ECI's backward-noise-resampling idea, plus logit-normal time sampling from Esser et al. 2024) applied to a new setting, which is incremental engineering rather than a fundamentally new method.

The 'Pareto-optimal' framing in the title is not rigorously substantiated: PBFM is a single fixed operating point (no tunable trade-off weight since ConFIG removes manual weighting), so there is no actual Pareto front traced out by the proposed method itself; claims of Pareto-optimality rest on visually comparing a single point against other single-point baselines rather than a principled multi-objective analysis.

In the flagship Darcy flow experiment (Table 2), the proposed PBFM method actually has worse distributional accuracy (WD 0.138) than the unconstrained FM-OT baseline (WD 0.059), more than doubling the Wasserstein distance, which directly contradicts the abstract's claim that 'physics constraints do not impede inference performance.'

Other baselines (PIDM-ME, PCFM) achieve substantially lower residual errors than PBFM in Darcy and Dynamic Stall settings, meaning PBFM does not strictly dominate competitors and the overall argument for its superiority depends on a somewhat subjective weighting of which metric matters more.

Training-time overhead is non-trivial (up to ~3x memory and ~2.5x wall-clock time with 4 unrolling steps), which could limit applicability to larger-scale models/foundation-model settings, an important limitation for a method intended as 'a practical tool for scientific machine learning.'

Results in the main tables lack uncertainty quantification (error bars/seed variance), making it difficult to assess whether reported differences (e.g., small WD or JS gaps between methods) are statistically meaningful.

Some baselines are evaluated with a different (UNet) backbone rather than the DiT backbone used for PBFM, and the appendix shows the backbone choice alone causes large differences in distributional metrics, raising concerns about whether comparisons in the main tables are fully fair/controlled for architecture.

The additional ablation splitting the physics residual into separate losses (PBFM 3-losses) shows no clear benefit and even worse WD, suggesting the specific design choices in the main method are somewhat ad hoc rather than well-motivated by a deeper principle.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing of the physics-vs-distribution trade-off as a Pareto optimization problem, which is a useful conceptual contribution distinguishing this work from prior physics-constrained generative modeling papers that report only single-metric improvements.

Principled combination of techniques: conflict-free gradient updates (ConFIG) to avoid manual loss-weight tuning, and unrolling to directly evaluate residuals on the final predicted sample rather than the posterior mean, explicitly targeting the theoretically motivated Jensen's gap issue.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three diverse and representative PDE benchmarks (steady-state Darcy flow, transient Kolmogorov flow, and complex multi-field dynamic stall with nonlinear analytic constraints), each with different residual computation strategies (finite differences, FFT, pointwise).

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies: unrolling step count vs residual error, FM integration steps, sigma_min sensitivity, power-law weighting of residual loss, stochastic vs deterministic sampling threshold, loss decomposition (3 losses vs combined), and a toy problem that builds intuition for each proposed component's contribution.

Strong quantitative results showing PBFM advances the Pareto front relative to many established baselines (FM-OT, PIDM-ME, CoCoGen, DiffusionPDE, D-Flow, ECI, PCFM) while maintaining competitive/negligible inference-time overhead compared to inference-time correction methods.

High practical significance demonstrated via a real-world CFD dynamic stall case (helicopter/wind turbine relevant), with dramatic speedup over a CPU-based numerical solver (76 minutes vs sub-second GPU inference), underscoring surrogate modeling value.
Transparent reporting of training-time compute/memory overheads (Table 6, 13) and explicit discussion of limitations, aiding reproducibility and honest positioning.
Good related-work coverage and a clear comparative taxonomy table (Table 1) situating the method against many recent physics-constrained generative approaches.
weaknesses: The core technical components (ConFIG, unrolling, logit-normal time sampling, stochastic noise resampling akin to ECI) are largely adapted from existing work rather than newly proposed; the primary contribution is their combination and application to the physics-constrained flow matching setting rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

"Pareto-optimal" is used somewhat loosely — the paper shows PBFM dominates or improves upon a set of compared baselines on the residual/WD trade-off curve, but does not rigorously verify proximity to a true Pareto front (e.g., via hypervolume metrics or exhaustive weight sweeps for baselines), and some baselines (e.g., PIDM-ME on Darcy) still achieve much lower residual error, meaning PBFM does not strictly dominate on every axis.

Comparisons across methods are partly confounded by architecture differences (PBFM uses DiT while some baselines like CoCoGen/PIDM use UNet per Bastek et al.), which is acknowledged but still complicates fully controlled comparisons.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-seed variance are reported for the main quantitative results tables (Tables 2, 4), limiting assessment of statistical significance of the reported improvements.

The claim of eliminating "manual loss balancing" is somewhat overstated, since the method still requires tuning several sensitive hyperparameters (unrolling steps/curriculum, sigma_min, power-law exponent p, stochastic sampler threshold t*), each shown in the appendix to materially affect performance.

All benchmarks are restricted to 2D fields; scalability to larger 3D or higher-resolution physical systems is not empirically demonstrated, leaving open questions about how training-time unrolling costs (shown to scale up to ~3x memory, ~2.5x time) would affect more demanding real-world settings.
Some evaluation tables have missing entries for certain baselines (e.g., PCFM not evaluated on Kolmogorov flow), reducing completeness of the cross-method comparison in that setting.
